close.title: Let’s Build the Way In.
close.sub: IP-extension partnerships · Co-productions with immersive in the plan from day one

a.title:
Old Stories,
New Doors
a.subtitle: What five winters of A Christmas Carol VR taught us about classic IP
a.thesis: Beloved stories need new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and screen. Live immersive theater is a working model for the audience half, and the right partnership supplies the rest.
a.takeaway: The curtain comes down. The story doesn’t have to.
a.cover_spoken: Pause. Walk to center, wait for quiet. Buonasera, and thank you for having me.

b.title:
Engine Mastery
× Craft
b.subtitle: Why the studios winning in immersive need both
b.thesis: The companies winning in immersive pair engine mastery with craft: photoreal work that runs on the hardware audiences actually have, built by people who know how to give an audience a role.
b.takeaway: Craft makes them care. Engineering makes sure they can.
b.cover_spoken: Pause. Walk to center, wait for quiet. Buonasera, and thank you for having me.

pool.title:
Every Beloved Story
Hits the Same Ceiling.
bullets: The run ends. The season closes. The house only has so many seats.
The audience that loves it is getting older, and the next one needs a new way in.
Classic IP needs new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and the screen.
pool.tags: IP value · Audience development · New revenue
pool.notes: Let me start with a problem everyone here knows. You have a story people love. But the run ends. The release window closes. The theater has only so many seats. And the audience that grew up with that story is getting older. So the question isn't whether the story still works. It does. The question is where the next audience meets it, and who pays for that meeting. Hands up if you've had that conversation this year. [pause] We spent five winters on that question, with one very old story. It's a story you all know.

pool.title: It Started as a Small Ask
pool.subtitle: Originally produced in association with Actors Theatre of Louisville · 2021
bullets: Actors Theatre of Louisville asked us for production assets: digital characters and some video.
We came back with a bigger idea: a full live production of A Christmas Carol, in VR.
They said yes, then gave us their blessing to remount it every year.
pool.notes: In 2021, Actors Theatre of Louisville called us. Their stage production of A Christmas Carol was adapted and directed by Robert Barry Fleming. They wanted production assets: some digital characters, some video. Not a VR show. We came back with a bigger idea. If we're building the sets, the characters and the costumes anyway, why not stage the whole thing, live, in virtual reality? They said yes. Then they gave us their blessing to remount it every year. The theater didn't hand off its story. It extended it, with a partner, into a new format.

pool.title: A Christmas Carol VR
pool.subtitle: Live actors. Live audiences. One shared virtual stage.
bullets: Live actors with face and full-body capture perform on the streets of a virtual Victorian London
Fully remote: actors, crew and audience each join from wherever they are
Five holiday seasons, 2021–2025 · The final run, December 2025: 15 performances
pool.notes: Here's what we made. A Christmas Carol, performed live, inside virtual reality. Two actors, Ari Tarr and Debbie Deer, play every role. They perform in Unreal Engine as MetaHumans, with face and full-body tracking, on the streets of a virtual Victorian London. David Gochfeld directed it for VR. The actors, the crew and the audience are all in different places, and they share one stage. About an hour, a curtain time, a house. We ran it five holiday seasons, 2021 through 2025. The number to remember: the final run, December 2025, played fifteen performances, plus a Christmas Eve replay streamathon. And every one of those nights was a real performance. If an actor improvised, the audience saw it.

pool.title: How Audiences Experienced It
pool.subtitle: Not watching a story. Standing inside one.
bullets: Eye contact: the actor sees you, and plays the scene to you
AI Dickens, a digital host voiced with the lead actor’s permission, welcomes guests before curtain
After the show, a live Q&A with the actors
pool.notes: So what did it feel like? Close. Scrooge can turn and look you in the eye, because the actor can actually see you. That changes how people watch. Before curtain, a digital host, AI Dickens, welcomes everyone. We built his voice from our lead actor's voice, with his permission, and we paid him for it. That lets the human save his energy for the show. After the show, the actors stay for a live Q and A. Nobody is watching a recording of a play. They're part of a night that happens once.

pool.title: What It Proved About Classic IP
bullets: A story audiences already love lowers the barrier to a brand-new format
A live show without a building: the house can be anywhere
The value outlived the run: characters, sets, an AI host and live-performance tools we reuse
pool.notes: What did five winters prove? One: familiarity is an asset. A story people already love makes a new format easier to try. Two: the house can be anywhere. A live show doesn't need a building, so the audience isn't limited to who can get to one. Three: the value outlived the show. The characters, the sets, the AI host and the live tools carried into our next projects. And I'll be honest about what it didn't prove. The work was strong, and it still needed a different funding and distribution model. It needed a partner who knows how its audience finds it. Those three lessons apply to any classic IP.
pool.subtitle: Five winters, three lessons

pool.title: XR Inside a Normal Film Pipeline
pool.subtitle: The crew uses the headset. The audience gets a normal film.

items.t:
Scout a scanned
location in VR

Try lenses, lights
and blocking at 1:1

Pull stills into
the shot list

Rehearse actors
in the virtual set

pool.notes: Most of you will never sell a ticket to a headset, and you don't have to. Here's XR inside a normal pipeline, where the result is still a film. Pre-production: scout a scanned location from anywhere, put a virtual camera in it, try lenses, lights and blocking at full scale, and pull stills into the shot list. Production: rehearse actors in the virtual space, the way we did with the Royal Shakespeare Company, capture performances onto digital humans, and see real-time previs. Post: because we recorded our Christmas Carol performances as data, a director can shoot new coverage after the show is over. Filled dots are things we've built. The hollow one, XR can do today. The audience never wears a headset. Think of it as better preparation, not a new format. ALEX TO CONFIRM: 'Try lenses, lights and blocking' and 'Pull stills into the shot list' credit the UOXR film kit (grabbable camera with 24-85 mm lenses and masks, monitor, film lights, A/B/C marks, Take still), built on 2026-10-21 and not yet merged: call it a prototype, and make those two dots hollow (al: false) if it is not in the demo area. Scouting cites the RSC's 1:1 Swan scan; capture cites Carol's MetaHumans; post cites the Carol replay and cinematographer builds. 'Real-time previs and virtual sets' is a general XR capability, not an Agile Lens credit.

pool.title:
Scan the Real Place.
Walk It Before You Fly.
pool.subtitle: Gaussian splats: a photoreal capture of a real location you can stand in

clips.alt: A Gaussian-splat scan of a fountain in a city square at night: scattered points resolve into a photoreal scene as the camera circles the fountain

rows.t: Capture a real place in minutes, with a phone or a scanner
Photoreal, view-dependent detail at human scale
Walk it in VR at 1:1: scout, block, try lenses, plan shots
Share the space with a remote director, DP or producer
Reuse it as a virtual-production backdrop or set extension
Lighter than a photoreal mesh; cheap to re-scan when the place changes

pool.notes: Let's talk about splats. Gaussian splats. [pause] This clip is a scan of a real square at night. Watch the dots turn into a place. [pause] For a production, that matters in a few ways. Capture takes minutes, with a phone or a handheld scanner, not weeks of modeling. The detail is photoreal, and it changes as you move, the way a real place does. And in a headset, you can stand in it at full scale: scout it, block it, try lenses, plan the shots, before anyone travels. We've done exactly that: our team scanned a hotel interior with a handheld scanner, and we have scans running on standalone headsets in our demo area. The hollow dots are what splats can also do: share the space with a remote director, become a backdrop for virtual production, and get re-scanned cheaply when the location changes. Two honest limits, if anyone asks: you need permission to scan a place and the people in it. And the files are big, so standalone headsets need trimmed scans. ALEX TO CONFIRM: the clip is your own and cleared; its place and capture method aren't evident from the frames, so the slide doesn't name them; name it on stage only if you want to and have permission. Filled dots rest on the KB: Josette's handheld-scanner hotel scan (PCVR demo, 2026-10-21) and the UOXR showcase splat level on Quest 3 and PICO; hotel and monument are left unnamed. 'Minutes' for capture is the vendor-adjacent PortalCam figure and phone-app claims, not our measurement. HOW TO ADD JOSETTE'S CLIP: compress it into media/video/ (ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -an -vf scale=540:-2 -c:v libx264 -crf 27 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart media/video/splat-josette.mp4, plus a poster jpg), then in talk/pitch.json replace this slide's clips[1].img '[FILL: Josette's splat clip]' with that path, fill in poster, alt and credit, and run python tools/build_pitch.py. pool.title: What a Splat Can’t Do (Yet)
pool.subtitle: Worth knowing before you plan a shoot around one

clips.alt: A still from the Gaussian-splat walkthrough of the fountain at night

cards.d: No moving people, no running water: it records one instant
Relighting is limited; you get the light you scanned
Scanning places and people needs permission
Cleanup and editing are still catching up

pool.notes: And to be honest about the limits, because someone in this room will ask. [pause] A splat is a frozen moment: no moving people, no running water. The light is baked in, so you live with the light you scanned. You need permission to scan a place, and the people in it. The files are big, so standalone headsets need trimmed scans. And the editing tools are still young. None of that stops you from scouting with one. pool.title:
Beautiful Demos Are Easy.
Shipping Them Isn’t.
bullets: Immersive work lives or dies in the gap between the trailer and the headset
Engine mastery: it runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually have
Craft: once they’re inside, they care
pool.notes: Most of you have seen a gorgeous immersive trailer for something that never reached an audience. Or it reached one, and it stuttered. That gap is where immersive projects live or die. The companies winning in this space do two things at once. Engine mastery: the work runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually own. And craft: once people are inside, they care. Either one alone isn't enough. I'm going to show you both halves, with work you can try in our demo area today.

pool.title: We teach the engine we build in
pool.notes: Engine mastery first. I've been an authorized Unreal Engine instructor since 2020. More than 300 classes taught, more than 40 courses written. The people who teach the engine are the people who build your project. That matters for you because when something breaks the night before opening, the person fixing it is the person who teaches other people how it works.

pool.title: Photoreal That Actually Runs
pool.subtitle: Heavy scenes, real hardware
bullets: We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets
That moved A Christmas Carol VR from gaming PCs to headsets audiences already own
Increasing access is worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives
pool.notes: Here's what engine mastery buys you. We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets. No gaming PC. In 2024 that moved A Christmas Carol onto headsets people already own. Our rule: increasing access is always worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives the trip. Here's what that took in practice. Heavy scenes, real-time lighting, two actors with full face tracking, and a frame budget that a headset can actually hold. We cut what the audience would never notice and kept what they would. The result was a show that a family could watch from their living room without buying anything new.

pool.title:
What Kind of Partnerships
Are We Looking For?
pool.tagline: Two kinds. Both start with a story you already own or produce.
pool.notes: Which brings me to our moderator's question. What kind of partnerships are we looking for? Two kinds. Both start with a story you already own or produce. I'll keep this part short and concrete, because it's the reason I'm on this stage. [pause] If either of these sounds like you, find me after this session, or in the demo area this afternoon.

pool.title: 1 · IP-extension partnerships
pool.subtitle: With producers and rights holders
pool.bigText:
Bring the story.
We’ll build the way in.
pool.bigCaption: An immersive edition of a world audiences already love: live, location-based, or at home
pool.notes: First: IP-extension partnerships with producers and rights holders. You bring a story world audiences already love. We design and build the immersive edition: a live performance, a location-based experience, or something people take home on a headset. The rights stay yours. The audience gets a new door. That's exactly how Carol began: a theater extending its holiday classic, with a partner. Think about the stories on your slate that already have an audience. A classic, a series with a loyal following, a film with a world people want to stand inside. Those are the ones that travel best into a headset. [click] And if you want to do ANOTHER adaptation of A Christmas Carol, please let us know.
pool.bgAlt: A Christmas Carol VR key art
pool.callout: Want to do ANOTHER adaptation of A Christmas Carol? Please let us know!

pool.title: 2 · Co-productions from day one
pool.subtitle: Immersive inside the financing and distribution plan
pool.bigText:
In the plan,
not bolted on after.
pool.bigCaption: Budgeted with the production: new windows, new audiences, assets that carry across formats
pool.notes: Second: co-productions where immersive is in the financing and distribution plan from day one. Not bolted on after picture lock. When the immersive edition is in the first budget, the digital sets, characters and performances get built once and used everywhere: previs, marketing, the edition itself. The immersive release becomes another window and another audience. That's the lesson Carol taught us. The experience was strong. What it needed was a partner with the audience and the distribution plan from the start. It also changes the conversation with financiers, because you're showing them two releases built from one set of assets.
